lead: After this unit you can read a control specification, choose an on-off, P, PI, PD or PID controller, tune it, and design lead, lag or lag-lead compensation using root locus or Bode plots. You can also convert a continuous PID law into a digital PID that runs at a fixed sampling period.
about: This unit covers control actions and compensators. Chapter 5.1 introduces on-off control, the simplest two-state action. Chapter 5.2 builds P, PI, PD and PID controllers from three actions: proportional, integral and derivative. Chapter 5.3 gives practical PID tuning rules. Chapters 5.4 to 5.6 design lead, lag and lag-lead compensators, first by phase and gain reasoning and then with combined needs. Chapter 5.7 compares root-locus and Bode design routes. Chapter 5.8 converts continuous PID to a sampled digital controller. Each chapter uses transfer functions and standard responses from earlier units, so the student can read a specification, choose a controller or compensator, compute its parameters, and check the result.

chapters.idea: An on-off controller drives the plant with only two outputs, switching at an error threshold so the output cycles around the set point.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in detail. Cover ideal relay: u=U<sub>max</sub> when e>0, u=U<sub>min</sub> when e<0; here e=r−y is error, r is reference, y is output, and U<sub>max</sub>, U<sub>min</sub> are the two outputs. Add hysteresis band ±h. Show first-order and second-order plant response, limit-cycle amplitude and period, effect of hysteresis on switching frequency, and relay modelling. Some syllabi call this two-position control.

figure.aria: A sawtooth plot of tank temperature rising from 60 to 62 degrees Celsius in 4 minutes and cooling back in 10 minutes, repeating.
figure.caption: Hysteresis band 60 °C to 62 °C gives a 14 min cycle.

chapters.example: A tank heater switches on at 60 °C and off at 62 °C. With the heater on the temperature rises at 0.5 °C/min; with the heater off it falls at 0.2 °C/min. Find the on time, off time, cycle time and duty cycle. Answer: on time 4 min, off time 10 min, cycle 14 min, duty cycle 4/14 = 28.6 %.
chapters.trap: Ignoring hysteresis predicts infinite switching; the real loop has a limit cycle, and average output is not the same as a linear gain.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 closed-loop block diagrams; Unit 2 first-order response.
chapters.leave: Relay describing-function analysis to Unit 7; Routh stability to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: P, I and D actions combine to shape transient response and steady-state error.
chapters.depth: Cover parallel PID: C(s)=K<sub>p</sub>+K<sub>i</sub>/s+K<sub>d</sub>s. Define K<sub>p</sub> as proportional gain (dimensionless), K<sub>i</sub> as integral gain (s<sup>−1</sup>), and K<sub>d</sub> as derivative gain (s). P acts on present error, I removes offset, D anticipates slope. Show effects on first-order and second-order systems: P reduces rise time but leaves offset; PI makes a type 1 plant type 2 and can slow response; PD adds damping; PID combines all three. Mention series and standard forms by name. Some syllabi call this the three-term controller.

figure.aria: An error signal feeds three parallel branches with gains Kp, Ki/s and Kd s, and the three branch outputs add before the plant.
figure.caption: P, I and D branches add to form the control signal.

chapters.example: For G(s)=1/(s(s+2)) with unity feedback, (a) find K<sub>p</sub> so the closed-loop damping ratio ζ=0.5; (b) with K<sub>p</sub>=4 and PI integral gain K<sub>i</sub>=1 s<sup>−1</sup>, find the steady-state error to a unit ramp. Answer: (a) s²+2s+K<sub>p</sub>=0 gives ω<sub>n</sub>=2 rad/s and K<sub>p</sub>=4; (b) the PI open loop is type 2, so ramp error is 0.
chapters.trap: Derivative action amplifies sensor noise; integral action winds up during saturation; PI does not remove ramp error for a type 0 plant.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 steady-state error and second-order damping; Unit 3 Routh test.
chapters.leave: Tuning rules to 5.3; digital PID to 5.8; state feedback to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Tuning rules set PID gains from measured plant behaviour instead of trial and error.
chapters.depth: Cover Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop tuning with ultimate gain K<sub>u</sub> and ultimate period P<sub>u</sub>, where K<sub>u</sub> is the proportional gain for sustained oscillation and P<sub>u</sub> is its period. Give PID formulas K<sub>p</sub>=0.6K<sub>u</sub>, T<sub>i</sub>=0.5P<sub>u</sub>, T<sub>d</sub>=0.125P<sub>u</sub>, K<sub>i</sub>=K<sub>p</sub>/T<sub>i</sub>, K<sub>d</sub>=K<sub>p</sub>T<sub>d</sub>. Give PI formulas K<sub>p</sub>=0.45K<sub>u</sub>, T<sub>i</sub>=P<sub>u</sub>/1.2. Mention open-loop reaction-curve tuning and Cohen-Coon by name only.

figure.aria: A flow from a plant step test to finding Ku and Pu, choosing a rule table, setting PID terms, and retesting.
figure.caption: Closed-loop tuning finds the ultimate gain, then sets PID terms from a rule table.

chapters.example: A plant under proportional control oscillates continuously at K<sub>u</sub>=8 and P<sub>u</sub>=4 s. Find Ziegler-Nichols PID settings K<sub>p</sub>, T<sub>i</sub>, T<sub>d</sub>, K<sub>i</sub> and K<sub>d</sub>. Answer: K<sub>p</sub>=0.6×8=4.8, T<sub>i</sub>=0.5×4=2 s, T<sub>d</sub>=0.125×4=0.5 s, K<sub>i</sub>=4.8/2=2.4 s<sup>−1</sup>, K<sub>d</sub>=4.8×0.5=2.4 s.
chapters.trap: K<sub>u</sub> is not the normal operating gain; using a gain that merely oscillates a little gives wrong P<sub>u</sub>; T<sub>i</sub> and T<sub>d</sub> are times, not K<sub>i</sub> and K<sub>d</sub>.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 transient response; chapter 5.2 PID structure.
chapters.leave: Advanced auto-tuning not covered; digital implementation to 5.8.

chapters.idea: A lead compensator adds phase near crossover to raise phase margin and speed the response.
chapters.depth: Lead compensator C(s)=K<sub>c</sub>(s+z)/(s+p) with p>z. Define z as zero (rad/s), p as pole (rad/s), K<sub>c</sub> as gain. Let α=z/p<1. Maximum phase φ<sub>m</sub>=sin<sup>−1</sup>((1−α)/(1+α)) occurs at ω<sub>m</sub>=√(zp). Bode design: required φ<sub>m</sub>=PM<sub>req</sub>−PM<sub>old</sub>+margin; set ω<sub>m</sub> at the new gain crossover; find z=ω<sub>m</sub>√α, p=ω<sub>m</sub>/√α; choose K<sub>c</sub> for gain. Root-locus lead design uses the angle criterion. Some syllabi call this phase-lead compensation.

figure.aria: A phase curve that rises to 40 degrees at 5 radians per second and then falls at higher frequency.
figure.caption: Peak phase 40° at 5 rad/s for z=2.33 rad/s and p=10.73 rad/s.

chapters.example: Design a lead compensator for G(s)=1/(s(s+2)) to place dominant closed-loop poles at s=−2±j2√3. Choose the zero at z=2 rad/s. Find the pole p and gain K<sub>c</sub>. Answer: p=4 rad/s and K<sub>c</sub>=16, so C(s)=16(s+2)/(s+4).
chapters.trap: A lead zero must be left of its pole (p>z); swapping them gives lag. Adding phase at the old crossover does not guarantee the new crossover stays there.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 root-locus angle criterion; Unit 4 Bode phase margin.
chapters.leave: Lag design to 5.5; combined design to 5.6; full Bode construction to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A lag compensator raises low-frequency gain relative to high frequency to reduce steady-state error while keeping phase margin.
chapters.depth: Lag compensator C(s)=K<sub>c</sub>(s+z)/(s+p) with z>p. Let β=z/p>1. Maximum phase lag φ<sub>m</sub>=sin<sup>−1</sup>((β−1)/(β+1)) occurs at ω<sub>m</sub>=√(zp). Bode design: set K<sub>c</sub> to meet steady-state error; place the zero one decade below the new crossover; place the pole at z/β; check phase margin. Root-locus lag design places a pole-zero pair near the origin. Define all terms.

figure.aria: A negative phase curve that reaches about minus 55 degrees near 0.158 radians per second and returns toward zero.
figure.caption: Maximum lag 54.9° at 0.158 rad/s for z=0.5 rad/s and p=0.05 rad/s.

chapters.example: A unity-feedback plant G(s)=1/(s(s+1)) must have unit-ramp steady-state error ≤0.1. (a) Find the minimum gain K. (b) With K=10, design a lag section with zero at 0.1 rad/s and high-frequency attenuation 1/7.1. Find the pole, β and K<sub>c</sub>. Answer: K≥10; β=7.1; p=0.1/7.1=0.0141 rad/s; K<sub>c</sub>=1/7.1=0.141, so C(s)=0.141(s+0.1)/(s+0.0141).
chapters.trap: Placing the lag zero near the gain crossover adds too much phase lag; forgetting K<sub>c</sub> leaves the loop gain wrong; β is greater than 1, not less.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 steady-state error; Unit 4 Bode gain margin; chapter 5.4 lead contrast.
chapters.leave: Combined lag-lead to 5.6; root-locus lag details to 5.7.

chapters.idea: A lag-lead compensator uses a lag section for steady-state error and a lead section for phase margin when one section alone is not enough.
chapters.depth: Lag-lead compensator C(s)=K<sub>c</sub>[(s+z<sub>1</sub>)/(s+p<sub>1</sub>)][(s+z<sub>2</sub>)/(s+p<sub>2</sub>)] with lead p<sub>1</sub>>z<sub>1</sub> and lag z<sub>2</sub>>p<sub>2</sub>. Design the lag part first for gain and steady-state error, then the lead part for phase margin in Bode form. In root-locus form, place the lag pair near the origin and the lead pair for the desired dominant poles. Keep the two frequency ranges separated by about a decade.

figure.aria: An error signal passes first through a lag section, then a lead section, then the plant.
figure.caption: Lag section fixes low-frequency gain; lead section adds phase near crossover.

chapters.example: A lag-lead compensator has lead zero 2 rad/s, lead pole 8 rad/s, lag zero 0.2 rad/s and lag pole 0.02 rad/s. Find the DC gain, high-frequency gain, phase at 4 rad/s, and K<sub>c</sub> for DC gain 1. Answer: DC gain=(2/8)(0.2/0.02)=2.5; high-frequency gain tends to 1; phase=36.8°−2.6°=34.2° at 4 rad/s; K<sub>c</sub>=1/2.5=0.4.
chapters.trap: Designing lead and lag for the same frequency makes their phases cancel; forgetting the DC gain product K<sub>c</sub>; placing the lag zero below its pole.
chapters.leave: Exact root-locus construction to 5.7; frequency-domain stability to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Root-locus design places closed-loop poles directly, while Bode design shapes gain and phase margins; both can realize lead and lag compensation.
chapters.depth: Compare two routes. Root locus uses angle and magnitude criteria to place dominant closed-loop poles; choose a lead zero and pole for phase, and a lag pair near the origin for gain. Bode uses phase margin, gain margin and gain crossover; lead adds phase and lag adds low-frequency gain. Steps: list specifications; choose route; design; verify with time response and margins. Some syllabi call this analytical design of controllers.

figure.aria: A specification feeds two parallel design routes, root locus and Bode plot, which both lead to a lead or lag compensator and then verification.
figure.caption: Two design routes reach a compensator and are checked against the specification.

chapters.example: For G(s)=1/(s(s+2)) with unity feedback, a lead C(s)=16(s+2)/(s+4) is proposed. (a) Check that s=−2+j2√3 is on the compensated root locus. (b) Find the gain crossover frequency and phase margin of the compensated open loop. Answer: (a) the angle condition gives −180°, so the point is on the locus; (b) L(s)=16/(s(s+4)), gain crossover ω=3.14 rad/s, phase margin=51.8°.
chapters.trap: A root-locus design that meets the pole location may miss the Bode margin; a Bode design that meets margins may move the dominant poles. Always verify both.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 root locus; Unit 4 Bode plots and margins; chapters 5.4 to 5.6.
chapters.leave: Nyquist criterion details to Unit 4; state feedback design to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A digital controller samples the error every T seconds and computes the control from a difference equation.
chapters.depth: Define T as sampling period (s), e[k]=e(kT), and u[k] as control at sample k. Digital PID positional form: u[k]=K<sub>p</sub>e[k]+K<sub>i</sub>TΣ<sub>j=0</sub><sup>k</sup>e[j]+(K<sub>d</sub>/T)(e[k]−e[k−1]), with K<sub>p</sub> dimensionless, K<sub>i</sub> in s<sup>−1</sup>, K<sub>d</sub> in s. Mention velocity form and anti-windup by name. Name backward difference and Tustin discretization. Rule of thumb: T should be small compared with the closed-loop rise time.

figure.aria: A reference and feedback meet at a sum, the error is sampled, a digital PID computes a value, a zero-order hold feeds the plant, and the sensor closes the loop.
figure.caption: The sampler and zero-order hold convert the continuous loop to a sampled-data loop.

chapters.example: A digital PID has K<sub>p</sub>=2, K<sub>i</sub>=3 s<sup>−1</sup>, K<sub>d</sub>=0.5 s and T=0.1 s. The errors are e[0]=1, e[1]=0.5, e[2]=0.2. Find u[2] using the positional form. Answer: u[2]=2×0.2+3×0.1×(1+0.5+0.2)+(0.5/0.1)(0.2−0.5)=0.4+0.51−1.5=−0.59.
chapters.trap: Forgetting T in the integral term or dividing by T in the derivative term changes the effective gains by a large factor; derivative kick and integral windup must be handled.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.2 PID structure; Unit 2 rise time for choosing T.
chapters.leave: z-transform stability and digital state-space design to Unit 6; saturation nonlinearity to Unit 7.
